did_you_know.text: Did you know? The opening verse is the psalm’s heading. It includes an instruction for the choir director, the phrase “Do Not Destroy,” and attribution of the psalm to David through the words “A Miktam of David.”
Did you know? The psalm opens with a rhetorical question addressed to human beings: Do those in authority truly speak justly and judge fairly? The question expresses criticism of unjust judgment.

Did you know? The poet presents a contrast between appearance and reality: the wicked speak of justice, but in their hearts they plan wrongdoing, and through their actions they promote violence in the land.

Did you know? The wicked are described figuratively as those who are “estranged from the womb” and “speak lies.” This poetic description emphasizes the depth of their corruption and deceit; it is not a biological statement.
Did you know? The behavior of the wicked is compared to a snake’s venom: their rage is dangerous and harmful. The image emphasizes the moral and social danger of their behavior.

Did you know? The snake is described as a “deaf cobra” that stops up its ears, while the wicked are portrayed as people who refuse to listen even to the voice of an enchanter. This emphasizes their refusal to heed warnings or be influenced.
Did you know? Using figurative language, the poet asks God to break their “teeth” and the “fangs of young lions”—that is, to neutralize the predatory and threatening power of the wicked.

Did you know? The poet uses several images of disintegration and disappearance: water spreading away, an arrow that does not function properly, and a snail dissolving as it moves. Together, these images express the wish that the wicked will lose their power and stability.
Did you know? In this verse, the image of a “stillborn child” is added to the earlier images. Together, they form a sequence of things that never reach fulfillment or do not last.

Did you know? After describing the downfall of the wicked, the psalm portrays the righteous person rejoicing when he sees the Lord’s vengeance. The verse presents the righteous person’s response within the framework of divine judgment.

Did you know? The closing verse summarizes the message: the deeds of the righteous are not meaningless and have “fruit”; moreover, people come to the conclusion that “there is a God who judges on earth.”
